steps.explain: Reversed order = restore. The USB file is now the source and running-config the destination.

steps.task: After a password recovery, set the configuration register back to its normal default.
steps.explain: 0x2102 is normal boot; leaving it at 0x2142 would keep skipping startup-config on every reload.

title: Watch Out For…
body: A cluster of exam questions is really testing whether you read command syntax and diagnostic output carefully rather than just recognizing keywords. These are the traps students fall into most often on this module.
keyPoints: copy [source] [destination] order matters: copy usbflash0:/file running-config restores FROM the USB drive, it does not back up TO it — reversing the two arguments is the classic wrong-answer bait.

A duplex mismatch needs two conflicting settings — both manually set to different modes, or one autonegotiating while the other is manually fixed at full-duplex. A pure speed mismatch alone does not cause it, and show cdp neighbors / show ip interface brief will not reveal the duplex setting — only show interfaces will.
SNMPv3 'auth' means authenticated but unencrypted; only 'priv' (authPriv) adds encryption. Don't assume auth implies privacy.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You've now got the full network management toolkit: discovering neighbors with CDP and LLDP, keeping clocks aligned with NTP, centralizing events with syslog, monitoring remotely with SNMP, and recovering a device you're locked out of. These are exactly the mechanics this module's questions test.
keyPoints: CDP is Cisco-only and on by default; LLDP is vendor-neutral (802.1AB), off by default, and needs lldp transmit and lldp receive enabled separately per interface.
NTP stratum: lower number is closer to the authoritative Stratum 0 source; show ntp associations detail shows master vs. client.
Syslog severity runs 0 (Emergency, most severe) to 7 (Debugging, least severe); logging trap {level} sets the minimum forwarded.
SNMPv3 security levels are noAuth, auth (authentication only), and priv/authPriv (authentication plus encryption); traps beat constant polling because they only fire on significant events.
Password recovery: confreg 0x2142 in ROMMON, reload, copy startup-config running-config, set a new password and save, then config-register 0x2102 to make it permanent.

title: Why Network Design Matters
body: Every enterprise network you'll ever touch is built on the same hierarchical skeleton: access, distribution, and core. This module is about knowing exactly which layer does which job, how to shrink the damage when something fails, and how protocols like FHRP and EtherChannel keep the network up when a single device or link dies. Get the layer roles and the failure-domain logic straight and most of this module's questions answer themselves.
keyPoints: Hierarchical design (access/distribution/core) is the backbone of Cisco's borderless switched network model.
The exam tests layer roles, failure domains, redundancy, FHRP, and EtherChannel — all pieces of the same design puzzle.

title: The Three-Tier Hierarchical Model
body: The recommended design splits the network into three layers, each with one clear job. The access layer is the edge — it connects end-user devices directly and can supply Power over Ethernet. The distribution layer aggregates those access connections, enforces policy and security like ACLs, and establishes the Layer 3 routing boundary. The core layer is the high-speed backbone that aggregates every distribution block for fast, redundant connectivity.
keyPoints: Access = end-user connectivity and PoE, at the network edge.
Distribution = policy/ACLs, aggregation, and the Layer 3 boundary, plus connections to other networks.
Core = high-speed backbone that aggregates all distribution blocks.

title: Two-Tier Collapsed Core: The Trade-off
body: Not every network needs three separate layers. A collapsed core design merges the core and distribution layers into a single device or layer, which is simpler and cheaper to buy and manage. The trade-off is that merging layers means a failure of that one device now affects a bigger chunk of the network — the resulting failure domain is larger than in a full three-tier design.
keyPoints: Collapsed core (two-tier) = core + distribution merged into one layer/device.
Cheaper and simpler than three-tier, but the failure domain gets larger.
Three-tier remains the recommended design when scale and fault isolation matter most.

title: Failure Domains and Redundant Design
body: A failure domain is the portion of the network affected when a critical device or link fails. The trick the exam loves: what actually shrinks a failure domain is deploying routers or multilayer switches in pairs, not simply buying a single bigger or more expensive device. A redundant power supply only protects against a power failure — if that same device fails for any other reason, everything it served still goes down.
keyPoints: Limiting failure domain size means redundant device/link pairs, not raw capacity.
A redundant power supply only guards against power loss, not other device failures.
No single point of failure — duplicate links, devices, and power — is the core redundancy principle.

title: FHRP: Keeping the Default Gateway Alive
body: End hosts point to one default gateway IP, so what happens when that router goes down? First Hop Redundancy Protocols solve this by letting two or more routers share a virtual IP and MAC address, so a router or link failure doesn't force every host to be manually reconfigured. HSRP is Cisco's proprietary version; VRRP is the open-standard equivalent; GLBP goes further and load-balances outbound traffic across all participating routers instead of relying on one active router.

rows.label: HSRP
cells: One active router forwards; standby waits

rows.label: GLBP
cells: Load-balances across multiple routers at once

keyPoints: FHRP = shared virtual IP/MAC address acting as the default gateway (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP).
HSRP is Cisco-proprietary; VRRP is the open-standard equivalent.
GLBP is the only one of the three that load-balances traffic across multiple gateway routers simultaneously.

title: EtherChannel: Bundling Links
body: EtherChannel bundles multiple physical switch links into a single logical link. That delivers two benefits at once: more aggregate bandwidth between switches, and built-in redundancy if one physical link in the bundle fails. Because Spanning Tree Protocol sees the whole bundle as one logical port, it doesn't block the extra physical links the way it would block a separate redundant link.
keyPoints: EtherChannel = multiple physical links treated as one logical link.
Delivers increased bandwidth and redundancy at the same time.
STP treats the bundle as a single port, so it never blocks the redundant links inside it.

title: Converged Networks, Device Selection, and the 2960
body: A converged network carries voice, video, and data over one shared infrastructure instead of three separate parallel networks, cutting installation and management cost and complexity substantially. Picking the right hardware for each layer comes down to cost, port density, port speed/type, forwarding rate, and features like PoE, redundancy, and Layer 3 support. The Catalyst 2960 is a common fixed-configuration access-layer switch, but on IOS versions before 15.x it supports only one active switched virtual interface (SVI) at a time.
keyPoints: Converged network = one infrastructure for voice, video, and data — lower cost and complexity.
Device selection factors: cost, port density/speed, forwarding rate, PoE, redundancy, Layer 3 support.
Catalyst 2960 (pre-15.x IOS): fixed-configuration access switch, only one active SVI.

title: Watch Out For...
body: A few traps show up again and again in this module's questions. Watch for answer choices that sound like redundancy but aren't — a spare power supply is not the same as a redundant device. Watch for layer functions getting swapped between access, distribution, and core in the answer choices. And watch for wireless-access questions that test what wireless does NOT do.
keyPoints: Failure domains shrink from redundant device/link pairs — not from a redundant power supply alone, and not from buying one bigger device.
Don't swap layer functions: only the core is the high-speed backbone; distribution handles policy/ACLs and connections to other networks; access just connects end devices and supplies PoE.
Wireless access benefits are flexibility, lower cost, and easier growth — it does not increase bandwidth, and it actually adds central points of failure rather than reducing them.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You've got the shape of hierarchical network design: what each of the three layers does, why collapsing core and distribution trades cost for a bigger failure domain, how redundancy actually shrinks failure domains, and how FHRP and EtherChannel keep the network available when a single device or link fails.
keyPoints: Access = end devices + PoE; Distribution = policy/ACLs/L3 boundary; Core = high-speed backbone aggregating distribution blocks.
Collapsed core (two-tier) is cheaper/simpler but enlarges the failure domain versus three-tier.
Failure domains shrink via redundant device/link pairs, not bigger single devices or a lone redundant power supply.
HSRP is Cisco-proprietary, VRRP is the open standard, GLBP load-balances across routers — all three share a virtual gateway IP/MAC.
EtherChannel bundles physical links for both bandwidth and redundancy without Spanning Tree blocking them.

title: Why Troubleshooting Methodology Matters
body: Every network eventually breaks, and how you approach the fix separates a five-minute resolution from an all-day outage. This module isn't about memorizing more commands — it's about picking the right process: which OSI layer to start testing at, how to tell a DNS problem from a real outage, and which show command actually gives you the answer. Master the method and the individual facts click into place.
keyPoints: Structured methods (top-down, bottom-up, divide-and-conquer) give you a repeatable process instead of guessing.
The same symptom can have very different causes — telling them apart is the whole game.

title: The Three Structured Methods
body: When you don't yet know where a problem lives, you pick a structured method and test outward from there. Top-down starts at the Application layer and works down — good when one app or many users are affected. Bottom-up starts at the Physical layer and works up — a safe default when the cause is totally unknown, since physical issues are common and quick to rule out. Divide-and-conquer skips straight to a layer based on an informed guess from the symptoms, then moves up or down depending on the result.

rows.label: Top-down
cells: Problem seems tied to one app or affects many users

rows.label: Bottom-up
cells: Root cause unknown — cheap to rule out physical first

rows.label: Divide-and-conquer
cells: Informed-guess layer, then up or down
A symptom already points toward a specific layer

keyPoints: Divide-and-conquer is defined by making an informed guess about the likely layer, not by where it starts.
There's no single 'correct' method — the choice depends on the symptoms you're handed.

title: Educated Guess: Know When to Skip Steps
body: The educated-guess (or 'shoot-from-the-hip') approach skips structured testing entirely and jumps straight to a likely cause based on experience and intuition. It can resolve issues fast, but only in the hands of a technician who has seen enough failures to trust their gut. A less-experienced administrator who tries to shortcut the process the same way risks wasting time chasing the wrong cause, so structured methods are the safer choice for them.
keyPoints: Educated guess is the fastest method, but only reliable for seasoned admins.
Less-experienced staff should default to a structured method — top-down, bottom-up, or divide-and-conquer.

title: Narrowing the Scope
body: Once you've gathered symptoms, the next step is narrowing the scope — deciding whether the problem lives at the core, distribution, or access layer before you start chasing specific equipment. This keeps you from wasting time testing devices that were never in the failure path. Only after you've narrowed the scope to a layer do you move on to pinpointing the specific device or link.

layers.label: Core layer
layers.sub: High-speed backbone — is the problem even here?

layers.label: Access layer
layers.sub: End-user ports — most everyday problems surface here

keyPoints: Scope narrowing happens after symptom gathering and before you touch specific hardware.
Identifying core vs. distribution vs. access is the checkpoint before pinpointing equipment.

title: Baselines: Knowing What 'Normal' Looks Like
body: A network baseline is a recorded snapshot of normal performance — throughput, CPU load, error rates — captured while everything is working correctly. Its entire purpose is comparison: without a baseline, you have no reference point to prove that today's sluggish performance is actually abnormal. Establishing a baseline before problems happen is what turns 'the network feels slow' into a measurable, provable fact.
keyPoints: A baseline's purpose is to detect abnormal conditions by comparing future measurements against it.
No baseline means no objective way to say performance has degraded.

title: Documenting the Network: Logical vs Physical Diagrams
body: You can't troubleshoot a network you can't picture, so documentation comes in two flavors. A LOGICAL topology diagram shows how traffic flows: IP addressing, interface identifiers, and connection types (LAN, WAN, point-to-point). A PHYSICAL topology diagram records the hardware reality: device type and model, OS/IOS version, cable type and identifier, and cable specification. Exam questions love to hand you a mixed list and ask which items belong on which diagram — sort them by asking 'is this about the traffic path, or about the box and the wire?'
keyPoints: Logical diagram: interface identifiers, IP addressing, connection type (LAN, WAN, point-to-point).
Physical diagram: device type, OS/IOS version, cable type and identifier, cable specification.
Rule of thumb: traffic path → logical; box and wire → physical.

title: CEF: Fast Forwarding Without Per-Packet Lookups
body: Cisco Express Forwarding is the default Layer 3 switching mechanism, and it works by pre-building two tables so the router never has to do a full route lookup for every single packet. The FIB (Forwarding Information Base) is pre-populated from the IP routing table, giving CEF the destination prefixes and next hops in advance. The adjacency table is pre-populated from the ARP table, supplying the Layer 2 rewrite (MAC address) information needed to actually forward the frame.

nodes.label: FIB lookup
nodes.sub: Next hop, built from the routing table

nodes.label: Adjacency table lookup
nodes.sub: L2 rewrite info, built from the ARP table

keyPoints: FIB comes from the routing table; adjacency table comes from the ARP table — a frequently tested pairing.
This proactive setup is what lets CEF forward at hardware speed instead of hitting the control plane per packet.

title: Commands That Isolate the Problem
body: A handful of commands cover most troubleshooting scenarios. ping {ip-address|hostname} tests basic Layer 3 reachability, and traceroute {ip-address|hostname} shows exactly which hop along the path is failing. show ip route and show interfaces confirm whether a destination is in the routing table and whether an interface has errors, collisions, or a duplex problem. For deeper live analysis, debug {feature} (e.g., debug ip nat) streams real-time internal events but should always be turned off with undebug all when you're done, since it is CPU-intensive.
keyPoints: show tech-support bundles many diagnostic show commands into one output, typically gathered for a Cisco TAC case.
show processes cpu identifies a specific process consuming excessive router or switch CPU.
show version reveals the IOS image location, version, configuration register value, and uptime.

title: Watch Out For…
body: The exam bank loves testing the fine print around these methods and symptoms. A few distinctions come up again and again and are easy to mix up under pressure — read carefully before picking an answer.
keyPoints: Ping to an IP succeeds but ping to the hostname fails: that's a DNS resolution problem, not a network outage or reachability failure — don't chase the wrong layer.

A duplex mismatch requires a duplex setting difference (both fixed differently, or one autonegotiating against a manually-fixed full-duplex side). A pure speed mismatch alone does NOT cause a duplex mismatch.

Asking a user to try an IP address instead of a URL is divide-and-conquer (an informed guess targeting DNS), not top-down — top-down means systematically testing the application itself rather than jumping straight to a layer-3/DNS test.

title: Ready to Troubleshoot
body: You now have the full troubleshooting toolkit: three structured methods plus educated guess, the symptom-gathering and scope-narrowing process, what a baseline is for, how CEF forwards packets, and the commands that isolate each kind of failure. These are exactly the ideas this module's questions test.
keyPoints: Divide-and-conquer means an informed guess at a layer, then moving up or down based on results.
CEF's FIB comes from the routing table; the adjacency table comes from the ARP table.
Ping to an IP works but ping to the hostname fails: that's a DNS problem, not a reachability problem.
A network baseline exists to detect abnormal performance by comparison to a recorded normal.
show tech-support aggregates diagnostics for TAC escalation; always disable debug output with undebug all when finished.

title: Why Network Virtualization Matters
body: Modern data centers don't buy a new physical server for every job anymore - they virtualize, they rent from the cloud, and they let a controller run the network. This module's questions are mostly word problems: a company describes a business need, and you have to name the exact technology that solves it - a hypervisor type, live migration, a cloud service model, or an SDN controller. Nail the vocabulary and the scenarios answer themselves.
keyPoints: Nearly every sample question here is a scenario - read for the underlying technology being described, not just surface keywords.
The module spans three big ideas: virtualization/hypervisors, cloud computing, and SDN (including Cisco ACI).

title: Hypervisors: Type 1 vs. Type 2
body: Virtualization decouples the OS from the physical hardware, letting several independent VMs run in parallel on one CPU - exactly how a data center can host a separate web server per customer on one physical box instead of a dedicated machine each. The hypervisor is the software (or firmware) that creates and manages those VMs. Cisco splits hypervisors into two types, and the exam wants the tradeoffs cold.

rows.label: Installed on
cells: Server hardware directly - no host OS

keyPoints: Type 1 = bare metal, installed straight on hardware; because it has no GUI or local OS of its own, it needs a separate management console.
Type 2 = hosted on top of an OS you already have (like VMware Fusion) - no management console, no direct hardware access.
If a question says 'no management console' and 'runs on an existing OS,' that's Type 2 every time - don't assume the fancier-sounding option is Type 1.

title: Live Migration and Disaster Recovery
body: Virtualization's other big exam angle is disaster recovery. Because a VM is abstracted from its physical hardware, live migration lets you move a running VM to a different - even geographically distant - physical host with minimal downtime. That hardware independence means the DR site doesn't have to match production hardware exactly, which is the piece the questions are really testing.
keyPoints: Live migration moves the running VM itself to another host, not just a copy of its data.
Hardware independence is why DR planning gets simpler with virtualization: the backup site can use different equipment than production.
A data center used purely as an offsite backup facility for company servers is a separate but related answer - it's the physical site, while virtualization/live migration is the mechanism.

title: Cloud Service Models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
body: Cloud computing gives on-demand access to a shared pool of resources without owning the equipment yourself - which is why it's the answer whenever a question is about cutting onsite IT/energy/facility costs, enabling telecommuting, or backing up a phone's photos from anywhere. The three service models differ in how much the provider manages for you.

layers.label: SaaS
layers.sub: Ready-to-use application; provider manages everything underneath

layers.label: PaaS
layers.sub: Platform and tools for developing and deploying apps

layers.label: IaaS
layers.sub: Virtualized compute, storage, and networking - customer still manages it

keyPoints: IaaS = infrastructure you still manage; PaaS = a development/deployment platform; SaaS = a finished application you just use.
Repeatedly tested cloud benefits: access data anywhere/anytime, fewer onsite IT equipment costs, streamlined operations by subscribing only to needed services.
A student backing up phone photos while studying abroad is the same underlying 'cloud services' answer as an enterprise using IaaS.

title: Cloud Deployment Models
body: Separate from the service model (what you get) is the deployment model (who it's shared with). The exam bank draws on all four: public cloud is open to anyone, private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, hybrid cloud mixes public and private, and community cloud is shared by organizations with common concerns.
keyPoints: Public = general-public, multi-tenant; Private = one organization only.
Hybrid = a deliberate mix of public and private; Community = shared among organizations with a common interest (e.g., similar compliance needs).
Don't confuse deployment model (public/private/hybrid/community) with service model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS) - they answer different questions.

title: SDN: Splitting the Planes
body: Traditional network devices bundle three jobs in one box: the data plane (actually forwarding packets), the control plane (deciding how to forward them), and the management plane (configuration and monitoring). Software-Defined Networking pulls the control plane out of every device and centralizes it in one SDN controller, which then programs the devices beneath it through APIs.
keyPoints: Data plane = forwarding hardware; control plane = routing/forwarding decisions (now centralized in the controller); management plane = device config/monitoring.
Northbound API: controller talks up to business/SDN applications, letting admins shape traffic and deploy services.
Southbound API: controller talks down to switches and routers to directly control them - south points down to the devices.

NFV is related but distinct: it moves network functions (firewall, router, load balancer, IDS/IPS) off dedicated appliances onto standard servers as software; SDN centralizes control, NFV virtualizes functions.

title: Cisco ACI and the Spine-Leaf Fabric
body: Cisco's concrete SDN implementation is ACI, built on a two-tier spine-leaf fabric: every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, but leaves never connect directly to each other. That design keeps every endpoint exactly one hop away from any other endpoint. The APIC controller is the 'brains' of ACI - it translates high-level application policies into the actual programming pushed out to the fabric.
keyPoints: Every leaf connects to every spine; leaves never connect to each other directly - any endpoint is always exactly one hop from any other.
APIC = the centralized controller that translates application policy into actual fabric programming - remember it as the 'brains' of ACI.
ACI is built on Nexus 9000 switches; it's Cisco's real-world example of an SDN architecture in practice.

title: Watch Out For…
body: A few distinctions get tested again and again in nearly identical wording, so slow down and identify exactly which term the question wants before you answer.
keyPoints: Type 1 vs. Type 2 hypervisor: 'no management console' plus 'runs on an existing OS' means Type 2, not Type 1 - don't assume the enterprise-sounding option is the right one by default.

SDN vs. NFV: centralizing routing decisions in a controller is SDN (control plane); turning a firewall/router/load-balancer appliance into software on a generic server is NFV. They complement each other but are not the same concept.
Cloud service model vs. deployment model: IaaS/PaaS/SaaS answers WHAT you're getting; public/private/hybrid/community answers WHO it's shared with - match the question to the right pair.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You've covered how data centers virtualize hardware, how the cloud packages and shares that virtualized capacity, and how SDN centralizes network intelligence with Cisco ACI as the concrete example. These facts cover most of what this module tests.
keyPoints: Type 1 hypervisors are bare metal (no host OS, need a management console); Type 2 hypervisors run on a host OS (no management console, no direct hardware access).
Live migration moves a running VM to another host with minimal downtime, giving disaster-recovery sites hardware independence.
Cloud service models are IaaS (infrastructure), PaaS (platform), SaaS (software); cloud deployment models are public, private, hybrid, and community.
SDN centralizes the control plane in a controller; northbound APIs talk to applications, southbound APIs talk to switches and routers.
Cisco ACI's spine-leaf fabric keeps every endpoint one hop apart and is centrally managed by the APIC controller.

title: Why Network Automation Matters
body: Modern networks are too big to configure one device at a time by hand. Automation shifts that work to scripts and APIs that push the same configuration to hundreds of devices at once, using data formats and web-style requests instead of typed CLI commands. This module's questions are heavy on syntax memorization — exact JSON punctuation, exact HTTP-verb-to-CRUD mapping — so precision matters more than intuition here.
keyPoints: Network programmability replaces manual, per-device CLI entry with centralized, script/API-driven configuration.
Three data formats (JSON, XML, YAML) and the REST API model are the backbone of this shift.

title: Data Formats: JSON, XML, YAML
body: Automation tools exchange configuration and state data in one of three formats, and each has its own punctuation rules. JSON encloses key/value pairs (an object) in curly braces { } and ordered lists (an array) in square brackets [ ], with double-quoted string keys separated from values by a colon. XML wraps every value in a matching pair of tags, like <tag>data</tag>. YAML drops the punctuation almost entirely — unquoted key: value pairs, with indentation instead of brackets or commas showing the structure.
keyPoints: Curly braces { } = a JSON object; square brackets [ ] = a JSON array — an ordered, comma-separated list of values.
JSON keys must be double-quoted strings; a colon separates each key from its value.
YAML's reliance on indentation (not brackets/commas) is why Ansible playbooks are written in it.

title: REST APIs and the Query String
body: REST/RESTful is by far the dominant API architecture — it accounts for more than 80% of web service APIs — because it runs over ordinary HTTP against addressable resources. When a client sends a RESTful request, the query portion of that request typically carries three things: the data format being requested (JSON, XML, or YAML), a key that authenticates the requester, and parameters that carry the request-specific data. APIs also come in public and private flavors: a private, or internal, API is exposed only within an organization, such as letting a company's own salespeople reach internal sales data from a mobile app.
keyPoints: REST/RESTful APIs make up over 80% of web service APIs — the most widely used web service API architecture.
A RESTful query string typically specifies: format, key (authentication), and parameters.
A private (internal) API serves only users/applications inside the organization, not outside parties.

title: HTTP Methods = CRUD
body: RESTful APIs perform Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations using five standard HTTP methods. This mapping is tested directly and repeatedly, so know it cold rather than reasoning it out under pressure.
keyPoints: POST creates a new resource; GET retrieves (reads) it.
PUT replaces/fully updates a resource; PATCH partially updates it — they are not interchangeable.
DELETE removes the resource.

title: URI, URL, and URN
body: A web resource reference breaks into three related terms. URI is the umbrella term for the complete reference — protocol, host, path, and fragment all together. URL is the protocol-plus-location you'd actually use to retrieve the resource. URN names the resource — host and path — without specifying a protocol. Take http://www.buycarsfromus.com/2020models/ford/suv.html#Escape: the protocol is http, the host+path form the named resource, the full address without the fragment is the URL, the complete reference including the fragment is the URI, and #Escape is just a fragment.
keyPoints: URI = the complete reference, including the fragment — the broadest of the three terms.
URL = protocol + host + path — what you'd use to fetch the resource, without the fragment.
URN = host + path only, naming the resource with no protocol attached.

title: Configuration Management Tools
body: Once devices can be reached via APIs, configuration management tools apply that automation at scale, and they split along two axes: agent-based vs. agentless, and push vs. pull. Ansible is agentless and push-based, using SSH and playbooks written in YAML. Puppet and Chef are both agent-based and pull-based — managed nodes periodically reach out to a central server to pull their configuration, with Puppet manifests and Chef recipes both written in Ruby. SaltStack is the flexible one: it can run agent-based, using a component called a 'minion,' or agentless, and it's primarily push-based using YAML.
keyPoints: Ansible = agentless, push, SSH, YAML playbooks.
Puppet and Chef = agent-based, pull, Ruby (manifests / recipes respectively).
SaltStack is the exception that can run either agent-based (minion) or agentless.

title: YANG, NETCONF, and RESTCONF
body: These three work together to standardize device configuration. YANG is a data modeling language — it defines the structure, syntax, and semantics of a device's configuration and state data, but it doesn't move any data itself. NETCONF is the protocol that actually reads and writes that YANG-modeled data, using XML-encoded remote procedure calls carried over SSH. RESTCONF does the same job through a REST-like HTTP interface instead, carrying that same YANG-modeled data as JSON or XML.
keyPoints: YANG defines the data model (structure/rules) — it is not itself a transport protocol.
NETCONF = XML-encoded RPCs over SSH.
RESTCONF = JSON or XML over HTTP, REST-style access to the same YANG-modeled data.

title: Watch Out For…
body: A handful of mix-ups account for most of the missed points on this module's questions. Slow down on these three before answering.
keyPoints: Don't flip JSON's brackets: { } curly braces hold an object (key/value pairs); [ ] square brackets hold an array (an ordered list of values) — questions test this in both directions.
PUT and PATCH are both 'update,' but PUT replaces the entire resource while PATCH only updates part of it — they are not interchangeable answers.
On a URL like http://host/path#fragment, the fragment (#Escape) belongs only to the URI — it is not part of the URL, not part of the URN, and 'page information' is a distractor, not a real term.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You now have the full toolkit for network automation: the three data formats and their punctuation rules, REST's HTTP-verb-to-CRUD mapping, how a RESTful query string is built, the URI/URL/URN distinction, and where each configuration management tool sits on the agent/push axis.
keyPoints: JSON: { } = object, [ ] = array; XML: <tag>data</tag>; YAML: key: value with indentation, no brackets or quotes.
CRUD to HTTP: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.
A RESTful query string carries format, key, and parameters; REST is used by over 80% of web service APIs.
Ansible = agentless/push/YAML; Puppet & Chef = agent/pull/Ruby; SaltStack = either model, mostly push/YAML.
NETCONF = XML over SSH; RESTCONF = JSON/XML over HTTP; both manipulate YANG-modeled configuration data.
